title: Waterfall plot
text:
Specific Use Case: Clinical Trials

In oncology, for example, a waterfall plot may be used to present each individual patient’s response to a particular drug based on a parameter, such as tumor burden. This graphic can represent the percent growth or reduction of the tumor by radiologic measurement (Gillespie TW. Understanding waterfall plots. J Adv Pract Oncol. 2012 Mar;3(2):106-11. PMID: 25031936; PMCID: PMC4093310.).
A waterfall plot is very often used to visualize biological data collected throughout a clinical trial. It provides a clear and concise representation of individual variations observed in biomarkers, pharmacokinetic concentrations, or other biological parameters measured over time.

title: Swimmer plot
section: Specific Use Case: Clinical Trials (TAKTIC clinical trial exemple)
text:
Specific Use Case: Clinical Trials (TAKTIC clinical trial exemple)

In the field of clinical trials, the swimmer plot is primarily used to depict each patient’s treatment exposure over time. It clearly highlights the evolution of disease status as well as the different therapeutic phases, such as treatment cycles, interruptions, dose adjustments, or protocol modifications.
A representative example of this type of visualization is presented in the TAKTIC study (A prospective, multicentre, uncontrolled, phase IB/II study of LY2780301, a p70S6K/AKT inhibitor, in combination with weekly paclitaxel in HER2‑negative advanced breast cancer patients). In this study, the swimmer plot illustrates, for each patient, the time on treatment—including exposure to LY2780301 and paclitaxel—RECIST 1.1 response, and the activation status of the PI3K/AKT/PTEN pathway.

title: MOSAIC
section: Specific Use Case: Clinical Trials and Adverse Events (CTC-AE)
text:
Specific Use Case: Clinical Trials and Adverse Events (CTC-AE)

In clinical trials, MOSAIC plots can illustrate the distribution of toxicity grades (CTC-AE) according to:

Patient sex (X-axis),
Randomization arm (grouping),
and Grades (0 to 5) expressed as percentages (Y-axis).



CTCAE code according to the CTC-AE classification of MEDRA


Grade 1: Mild
Grade 2: Moderate
Grade 3: Severe
Grade 4: Life-threatening
Grade 5: Death related to adverse event


This approach allows you to:

Quickly visualize safety profiles across treatment arms,
Detect potential sex-related differences,
and communicate safety data effectively in an intuitive format.

For example a Mosaïc plot showing that, in the experimental arm, females have a higher proportion of grade 2–3 adverse events compared to males may guide further analysis toward specific risk factors.

title: Clinical Graphics
text:
Objectives

The purpose of this work is to present a set of essential graphical representations that support the execution of high-quality clinical trials. All examples are derived from datasets structured according to CDISC (Clinical Data Interchange Standards Consortium) standards in ADaM (Analysis Data Model) format, ensuring compliance with regulatory and industry requirements. The visualizations are implemented using R, Python3, and SAS to demonstrate versatility and adherence to best practices in clinical data analysis.
Data has been generated with random.cdisc library of the CRAN in R (Version 4.2.0). Specifically, data used are :


adsl: Subject-Level Analysis Dataset (ADSL)
adae: Adverse Event Analysis Dataset (ADAE)
adrs: Response Analysis Dataset (ADRS)
adlb: Laboratory Data Analysis Dataset (ADLB)
adtte: Time-to-Event Dataset (ADTTE)
adex: Exposure Analysis Dataset (ADEX)

What is a Study flux diagram in clinical trial
In clinical trials, the flow diagram of study populations illustrates the path of participants from their inclusion in the study to the different analysis sets used for statistical evaluation. This diagram provides a clear view of the actual numbers involved, the exclusions, and the potential impact of these changes on the robustness of the analyses.
In Phase I (objective: assess safety, tolerability, and pharmacokinetics), the diagram shows the participants included, those who received at least one dose of the investigational product, and any early discontinuations. The focus is on actual exposure, which is essential for defining the safety population.
In Phase II (objective: provide initial evidence of efficacy and refine dosing), the diagram displays the participants included, those potentially randomized depending on the study design, those treated, participants with evaluable efficacy data, and the reasons for withdrawal or exclusion from analyses. For randomized studies, the representation must follow the CONSORT flow diagram, an international standard structured into four stages (inclusion, allocation, follow‑up, analysis). CONSORT applies only to randomized trials; non‑randomized studies use a standard population flow diagram instead.


Population sets


The ICH E3 and ICH E9 guidelines define several key statistical populations required for regulatory analyses:



Primary Criteria Analysis Set: participants with the necessary data to evaluate the primary efficacy endpoint.


All Patients Set: all participants included in the study.


Full Analysis Set (FAS): a population close to the intention‑to‑treat principle, including participants who received at least one dose or who have at least one evaluable efficacy measurement.


Safety Set: all participants who received at least one administration of the study treatment, forming the basis for safety and tolerability analyses.



These elements ensure transparency, methodological consistency, and alignment with international regulatory standards in clinical study reports and scientific publications.


Exemples


Exemple

Note



Graphics has been built with the ADSL table. Data has been generated with random.cdisc librairy of the CRAN in R (Version 4.2.0).








Important



To generate our CONSORT flow diagrams in SAS, we rely on the open‑source project sas‑consort‑sgplot, available on GitHub. This project provides a simplified implementation of the original SAS programs developed by Prashant Hebbar and Sanjay Matange, as presented in their PharmaSUG 2018 paper CONSORT Diagrams with SG Procedures. Their work demonstrates how to construct publication‑quality CONSORT diagrams using SAS SG procedures and has become a widely referenced approach within the clinical programming community.
The GitHub project sas‑consort‑sgplot builds upon and streamlines the methodology described in the PharmaSUG article, offering a more straightforward and modular set of SAS macros. These improvements facilitate the creation of CONSORT diagrams while reducing programming complexity.
To write this page, we re‑use, adapt, and extend this simplified macro framework to meet the specific constraints of our clinical studies.

title: Lexis Diagram
text:
Why Use a Lexis Diagram



Detect inconsistencies: Quickly identify data entry errors (incorrect dates, wrong status, missed or delayed visits)


Monitor recruitment dynamics: Visualize the pace of patient enrollment and spot potential delays. Plot the inclusion curve: In addition to individual timelines, the diagram can display the overall trend of patient recruitment over time


Check protocol compliance: Highlight missed visits, delays in status updates, or deviations from the planned schedule


Gain an overview of data quality: acilitate a global assessment of trial progress and adherence to protocol


In summary, the Lexis diagram is a powerful tool to anticipate issues, improve data quality, and enhance communication among teams. Regular use, especially before DSMB meetings, contributes to better trial governance.

title: Lexis Diagram
text:
Advantages



Visual clarity and speed: Summarizes complex information in an intuitive graphic


Time-saving: Enables quick analysis without navigating large tables


Monitoring support: Helps monitoring teams focus on patients or sites requiring special attention


Preparation for DSMB meetings: Before a Data Safety Monitoring Board review, the Lexis diagram provides a consolidated view of inclusions and protocol adherence, enhancing transparency and discussion quality

title: Lexis Diagram
text:
Limitations



Complexity in large trials: Readability may decrease with a high number of patients


Dependent on data quality: The diagram is only reliable if data entry is accurate and complete


Descriptive tool: It complements statistical analyses but does not replace them

title: Tornado
section: Specific Use Case: Clinical Trials and Adverse Events (CTC-AE)
text:
Specific Use Case: Clinical Trials and Adverse Events (CTC-AE)

In the context of Adverse Events (AE) data, the tornado plot helps to illustrate the impact of various factors according to treatment groups and severity levels on the occurrence or frequency of adverse events. It is particularly useful for identifying the most influential variables and understanding how they contribute to the overall safety profile of a treatment. By presenting this information in a clear, hierarchical manner, the tornado plot enables clinical researchers to prioritize risk factors and make informed decisions regarding patient safety and treatment efficacy.
On the (Ox) axis are rapresented the pourcentage of adverse events and on (Oy) axis are rapresented different adverse events class. Results are presenting according of the randomized arm.
To create a tornado plot, you must have the Adverse Events table and the ADSL tables. These tables must be in CDISC format, structured according to the ADaM data model.
In the AE table, Adverse events must be coded according to the CTC-AE (Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events) classification.



CTCAE code


Grade 1: Mild
Grade 2: Moderate
Grade 3: Severe
Grade 4: Life-threatening
Grade 5: Death related to adverse event

title: Sankey diagram
section: Specific Use Case: Clinical Trials and Adverse Events (CTC-AE)
text:
Specific Use Case: Clinical Trials and Adverse Events (CTC-AE)

In clinical trials, a Sankey diagram can serve as a valuable tool for exploring the dynamics of subpopulations, for example when analyzing adverse events (AEs). It can illustrate participant transitions with respect to AE severity, suspected causality, or medical category, and can help visualize how certain subgroups evolve differently across the axes under study.
One major advantage of this approach is its ability to reveal particular trajectories, such as patients experiencing recurrent severe AEs or belonging to specific symptom clusters, thereby supporting the identification of subpopulations that may warrant closer examination. However, this method also has limitations, especially when data disparities between axes create numerous crossing flows, potentially leading to a visually complex or confusing representation.
The objective of a Sankey diagram in a clinical context must therefore be carefully defined beforehand, as its usefulness strongly depends on data structure, selected granularity, and the specific question being addressed by the user. When well designed and applied with discernment, it remains a powerful tool for summarizing multidimensional patterns related to safety outcomes or the clinical evolution of a study population.
Another graphics in relation with the Sankey diagram is the Alluvial plot.
